math-units: Work in SI units (m, kg, s). Convert by multiplying by fractions equal to 1 so the unwanted unit cancels, use each factor twice for an area, and keep as many significant figures as the least precise data, rounding once at the end.
scalars-vectors: Scalars have a size only; vectors have a size and a direction, which along a line is the sign. Displacement is the final minus the starting position; distance is the path length. Speed is the magnitude of velocity, and vectors on a line add as signed numbers.
math-symbols: Symbols stand for quantities with units, subscripts are labels and Δ means final minus initial. Rearrange by undoing operations in reverse order on both sides, solve in symbols first, then substitute numbers with units and check the units of the result.
motion-quantities: Average velocity is displacement over time, Δx/Δt, and average acceleration is change in velocity over time, Δv/Δt. Acceleration is any change in velocity and points along Δv: with v, the object speeds up; against v, it slows down. Instantaneous values are averages over very short intervals.
math-proportional: Functional dependence says how one quantity responds when another changes. Directly proportional: the same factor. Inversely proportional: divide by the factor. Square: the factor squared. For several changes, multiply their factors.
math-slopes-areas: Label every axis with a quantity and unit. The slope of a line is Δy/Δx between two points on it, with units (y unit)/(x unit); the area under a graph is height × width, with units (y unit) × (x unit). Fit a line to data, and linearize a curved relationship before fitting.
motion-representations: Motion can be shown as a motion diagram, x-t, v-t and a-t graphs, equations and words. Slopes go down the chain (x-t to v-t to a-t) and areas go up it. For constant acceleration, three kinematic equations apply, each missing one quantity; free fall is constant acceleration g downward.
reference-frames: Every velocity is measured relative to a reference frame. Along a line, a velocity relative to the ground is the velocity relative to a moving frame plus that frame's velocity; swapping observers flips the sign. Frames moving at constant velocity relative to each other agree on accelerations.
math-trig-components: A vector at an angle is the hypotenuse of a right triangle. The component adjacent to the given angle is A cos θ and the opposite one is A sin θ; the magnitude is the square root of the sum of the squared components. Add vectors by components, with the calculator in degree mode.
motion-2d: Two-dimensional motion is two independent one-dimensional motions sharing the same time. A projectile keeps a constant horizontal velocity v cos θ and falls freely with vertical acceleration g; the vertical motion sets the time of flight, and the range is the horizontal velocity times that time.
systems-center-of-mass: Choose a system and its boundary; when its insides do not matter, model it as one point at its center of mass, the mass-weighted average position x_cm = Σm·x ÷ Σm, which lies nearer the heavier parts and on any line of symmetry.
forces-fbd: A force is an interaction between two objects. To draw a free-body diagram, list every object touching your object plus Earth, and draw each force as a whole arrow from a dot, labeled with type and agent; the net force is their vector sum and is never drawn as an extra arrow.
third-law: Forces come in third-law pairs: equal in size, opposite in direction, same type, acting on two different objects, so they never cancel each other. Inside a chosen system the pairs are internal and add to zero; an ideal string carries one tension over an ideal pulley.
first-law: Newton's first law: zero net force means constant velocity, including rest. Translational equilibrium is ΣF = 0, checked direction by direction; inertia is a property, not a force; and the law holds in inertial frames, such as the ground.
second-law: Newton's second law: the acceleration of a system's center of mass equals the net external force divided by its mass, a = ΣF/m, and points along the net force. Apply it one direction at a time; for connected objects, use the whole system for the acceleration and one object for the tension.
gravitational-force: Every two masses attract with |F_g| = Gm₁m₂/r², measured center to center; the field g = F/m is about 9.8 N/kg at Earth's surface. A scale reads the normal force, the apparent weight, which differs from mg whenever the object accelerates and is zero in free fall.
friction: Friction acts along a surface. Kinetic friction, while sliding, is μ_k F_N and opposes the sliding; static friction, while gripping, is whatever prevents slipping, up to μ_s F_N. Usually μ_s > μ_k. Find the normal force first, since it is mg cos θ on a ramp and changes with tilted pulls.
spring-forces: An ideal spring exerts a force proportional to its stretch or compression from its relaxed length, F_s = −kΔx, always back toward the relaxed length; the spring constant k (N/m) is the slope of force against stretch, and a hanging mass at rest stretches it by mg/k.
circular-motion: Circular motion at constant speed is accelerated motion: a_c = v²/r toward the center, with v = 2πr/T. Real forces (tension, friction, normal force, gravity) must add to a net force mv²/r toward the center; for circular orbits this gives v = √(GM/r) and T² ∝ r³.
kinetic-energy: Kinetic energy is K = ½mv², in joules. It is a scalar, never negative, independent of direction and dependent on the reference frame. Because the speed is squared, doubling the speed quadruples K; and a change in K is ½mv_f² − ½mv_i², not ½m(Δv)².
work-by-forces: Work is W = F d cos θ: energy carried into an object (positive) or out of it (negative) by a force along a displacement. Perpendicular forces do none. The net work equals ΔK, and a varying force's work is the area under its force-position graph.
potential-energy: Potential energy is stored in the configuration of interacting objects and belongs to the system. ΔU_g = mgΔy near Earth, U_s = ½k(Δx)² for a spring, U_G = −Gm₁m₂/r far away. Only conservative forces have one; the zero is a free choice because only changes matter.
energy-conservation: Pick the system first. Inside it energy changes form; across its boundary it moves as work by external forces. With no external work and no friction, K + U is constant. Friction turns mechanical energy into thermal energy, and energy bar charts must add up to match the equation.
power: Power is how fast energy is transferred: P = W/Δt in watts, or P = F_∥v at an instant. The same work in less time means more power; at constant power a faster object gets a smaller force. A kilowatt-hour is a unit of energy.
linear-momentum: Momentum p = mv is a vector along the velocity. A system's momentum is the vector sum of its parts, and its center of mass moves at v_cm = Σp/Σm. In collisions and explosions the internal forces dominate, so the momentum just before equals the momentum just after.
impulse: Impulse J = F_avg Δt is the area under a force-time graph, and it equals the change in momentum. A fixed change in momentum spread over more time needs less force. The slope of a momentum-time graph is the net force.
momentum-conservation: Internal forces cancel in pairs, so only external forces change a system's momentum. With zero net external force, total momentum and the center of mass's velocity stay constant. Choosing the system decides which forces are external; always state the condition.
collisions: Collisions conserve momentum when no net external force acts. Elastic collisions also keep the total kinetic energy; inelastic ones lose some; perfectly inelastic ones stick and lose the most. Start every collision from momentum, and use energy only when the collision is elastic or after it is over.
rotational-kinematics: Rotation about a fixed axis is described by the angle θ in radians, the angular velocity ω = Δθ/Δt and the angular acceleration α = Δω/Δt, each with a sign for clockwise or counterclockwise. Every point of a rigid system shares them, and for constant α the three linear kinematic equations hold with θ, ω and α in place of x, v and a.
linear-rotational-link: A point a distance r from the axis of a turning rigid object travels s = rθ, moves at v = rω and has tangential acceleration a_T = rα, with angles in radians. All points share θ, ω and α, but points farther out move farther and faster. A string or belt that does not slip moves with the rim it touches.
torque: Torque measures how well a force turns an object about an axis: τ = r⊥F = rF sin θ, where the lever arm r⊥ is the perpendicular distance from the axis to the force’s line of action. Torques carry a sign for clockwise or counterclockwise and add to a net torque. A force diagram draws each force where it acts.
rotational-inertia: Rotational inertia I measures how hard an object is to set turning about an axis. For point masses I = Σmr², so it depends on both the mass and how far the mass is from the axis, with distance counted squared. The inertias of standard shapes are given. About an axis a distance d from the center of mass, I = I_cm + Md².
rotational-equilibrium: An object is in rotational equilibrium when the net torque on it is zero, so its angular velocity stays constant; it is in translational equilibrium when the net force is zero. A static object needs both. Take torques about the point where an unknown force (such as a hinge force) acts, and remember that a hinge force can point in any direction.
rotational-second-law: Newton’s second law in rotational form says α = τ_net/I: the net torque sets the angular acceleration, and a larger rotational inertia means a smaller α. Systems with a pulley that has mass need both the translational law for each block and the rotational law for the pulley, linked by a = Rα; the string’s tension is then less than a falling block’s weight.
rotational-kinetic-energy: An object turning about an axis has rotational kinetic energy K = ½Iω², the sum of ½mv² over all its pieces. It is a scalar in joules, is present even when the center of mass is at rest, grows with the square of ω and in proportion to the rotational inertia.
torque-work: A torque that turns an object through an angle does work W = τΔθ (angle in radians), or the area under a torque-angle graph when the torque varies. The net work done on a turning object changes its rotational kinetic energy; a torque that opposes the turning does negative work.
angular-momentum: Angular momentum is L = Iω for a rigid object turning about a fixed axis, and L = rmv sin θ for a point object about a chosen point. A net torque acting over a time changes it: angular impulse τΔt = ΔL, the area under a τ-t graph, and the net torque is the slope of an L-t graph.
angular-momentum-conservation: A system’s total angular momentum stays constant when the net external torque on it is zero. When the system changes shape, its rotational inertia changes and its angular velocity changes the opposite way (I₁ω₁ = I₂ω₂), while kinetic energy does not stay constant. Around a pivot, angular momentum about the pivot is conserved in a collision even though linear momentum is not.
rolling: An object rolling without slipping has v_cm = Rω, and its kinetic energy is ½Mv² + ½Iω². Static friction makes it spin without doing work, so mechanical energy is conserved: from rest down a height h, v = √(2gh/(1 + I/MR²)), which depends on shape only. When an object slips, v_cm ≠ Rω and kinetic friction dissipates energy until rolling sets in.
orbits: For a satellite of small mass orbiting a massive body, total mechanical energy is conserved (gravity is the only force, and it is conservative) and angular momentum about the central body is conserved (gravity exerts no torque about its center). In a circular orbit K = GMm/(2r) and E = −K; on an ellipse, K and U trade and the satellite is fastest at its closest point. Escape needs E = 0, v = √(2GM/r).
shm-intro: Simple harmonic motion is periodic motion driven by a restoring force proportional to the displacement from equilibrium and opposite to it (F = −kx); the force and acceleration are zero at equilibrium and largest at the amplitude, and a pendulum at small angles is a close match.
shm-period: The period of a block on a spring is T = 2π√(m/k) and that of a small-angle pendulum is T = 2π√(ℓ/g); neither depends on the amplitude, the pendulum's period does not depend on the bob's mass, and f = 1/T.
shm-representations: SHM is described by x = A cos(2πft) or A sin(2πft); on the graphs, speed is greatest and acceleration zero at equilibrium, speed zero and acceleration greatest at the turning points, and the period is independent of the amplitude.
shm-energy: With no friction the mechanical energy of an oscillator is constant: for a block on a spring E = ½kA², all potential at the turning points and all kinetic at equilibrium; doubling the amplitude quadruples the energy.
density-fluids: Fluids (liquids and gases) flow because their particles can move past one another; density ρ = m/V is a property of the material, and an ideal fluid is incompressible and nonviscous, so its density is constant.
fluid-pressure: Pressure is perpendicular force per area, a scalar in pascals; in a fluid at rest the absolute pressure is P = P₀ + ρgh, set only by depth, and the gauge pressure (what gauges read) is ρgh.
buoyancy: The buoyant force is the fluid's net upward push, caused by pressure increasing with depth; it equals the weight of the displaced fluid, ρ_fluid V_displaced g, and Newton's laws with buoyancy and gravity as separate forces decide whether an object floats, sinks or accelerates.
fluid-flow: For an ideal fluid in a full pipe, continuity (A₁v₁ = A₂v₂, mass conservation) sets the speeds and Bernoulli's equation (energy conservation per volume) then sets the pressures; faster flow at the same height means lower pressure, and a hole a depth h down gives v = √(2gh).
